itineraries.title: Mekong Isan in 8 Days: That Phanom, Pha Taem, and Ubon
itineraries.subtitle: In 8 days, follow the Mekong from Nakhon Phanom to Khong Chiam, then finish in Ubon Ratchathani.
itineraries.notes: Sam Phan Bok emerges only during the dry season, roughly from December to May, while the river’s two colors at Khong Chiam are most visible during the rainy season. All stops remain outside the 50 km strip along the Cambodian border, where France Diplomatie strongly advises against all travel.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: November to February, with highs of 31 to 32 °C in Ubon Ratchathani and almost no rain. Avoid April, the hottest month (average highs of nearly 37 °C), followed by the monsoon from May to September, the wettest period. Sam Phan Bok is visible only during the dry season, roughly from December to May.

map_keywords: Ho Chi Minh House Nakhon Phanom

visits.text: Modest but steeped in history, Ho Chi Minh’s house stands in the village of Ban Na Chok, 4 km from downtown Nakhon Phanom. The future leader of Vietnam lived here in exile in 1928 and 1929, among Vietnamese people who had settled in the region. The wooden stilt house, renovated in 2001, displays photographs and documents from that period. A memorial with a bronze statue stands in the same village. Admission is free. Come by taxi or bicycle, as no buses serve the site.

With yellow walls and a facade facing the Mekong, the Governor’s Residence Museum occupies a French colonial-style house built between 1912 and 1914. This style appears throughout the city, which faces former French Indochina. Inside, old photographs of Nakhon Phanom often have English captions. One bedroom remains furnished as it was for the visit of King Bhumibol and Queen Sirikit on November 12, 1955. The museum is open Wednesday through Sunday, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Wat Okat is a temple facing the Mekong, just steps from the Indochina Market. It houses two small seated Buddha statues, Phra Tiu and Phra Thiam, each about 60 cm tall. Local people believe their wooden originals date back to the 7th century. Every year, the statues are bathed during a ceremony on the full moon of the sixth lunar month, around May. Enter the sanctuary barefoot, with your shoulders and knees covered.

A Catholic church in a city of temples, St. Anne’s Church in Nong Saeng was built in 1926 on the banks of the Mekong. Its two towers are connected by a footbridge. Inside, light filters through colorful stained-glass windows. Avoid Mass times when visiting, or remain quietly at the back if a service is taking place.

activities.text: Walk along Nakhon Phanom’s Mekong promenade at sunrise, with Laos on the opposite bank. It forms part of the 70 km Sawan Chai Khong trail, which runs south to Wat Phra That Phanom. On the riverbank stands the statue of Phaya Si Sattanakharat, installed in 2016. It depicts a seven-headed naga. In local beliefs, the naga is a legendary serpent associated with the Mekong. On Friday through Sunday evenings, a pedestrian street beside the river turns into a market.

practical_info.tip: Nakhon Phanom Airport, served by Thai AirAsia and Thai Lion Air from Bangkok’s Don Mueang Airport, is 13 km west of downtown. Rent your car there and check that the agency allows you to return it at Ubon Ratchathani Airport.

activities.text: If you still have energy at the end of the day, watch the sunset from the river aboard the Mekong Paradise Cruise. According to the Bangkok Post in 2021, this restaurant boat departed every evening at around 5:30 p.m. for about 2 hours. The ticket covered the cruise, but food and drinks were extra. The departure point is near the Indochina Market and Wat Okat.

practical_info.tip: Check at the dock the day before to confirm that the cruise still runs and what time it departs, as this information dates from 2021.

visits.text: In 1975, That Phanom’s great stupa collapsed. Its replica at Wat Phra That Renu shows what it looked like. A stupa is a spire-shaped Buddhist monument that houses relics. This one was erected in 1918 as a smaller version of That Phanom’s: about 35 m tall, white and gold. Admission is free during the day. Allow 45 minutes before continuing to That Phanom, 15 km to the south.

activities.text: You can buy Phu Thai textiles right on the grounds of Wat Phra That Renu. This community in Renu Nakhon is known for its handwoven silk and cotton. On Saturday evenings, a market sets up around the temple. You’ll find indigo-dyed fabrics, matmi (fabric whose threads are dyed before weaving), and embroidered clothing. During the week, walk through the village to see the looms.

practical_info.tip: On Saturday, arrive in the late afternoon for the market, then stay overnight in That Phanom, a 20-minute drive away.

visits.text: Gold leaf, lotus buds, and monks’ chants: at Wat Phra That Phanom, the great golden stupa rises more than 50 m. It is the province’s main Buddhist shrine. According to tradition, it holds a chest bone of the Buddha. On August 11, 1975, after several days of heavy rain, the tower collapsed. It was rebuilt and reopened in 1979. A small museum displays photographs of the collapse. Come at dawn, between 5 a.m. and 7 a.m., when the monks make their rounds to receive food offerings. Cover your shoulders and knees.

Wat Hua Wiang marks the northern end of That Phanom’s riverfront. The temple’s age is unknown. Its ordination hall, where novices become monks, was built between 1917 and 1921. Its interior walls are painted. Stop by as you follow the Mekong, before or after visiting Wat Phra That Phanom. Admission is free; wear clothing that covers your shoulders and knees.

activities.text: Walk down from Wat Phra That Phanom toward That Phanom’s riverfront, passing beneath a kind of triumphal arch set in the middle of a traffic circle. Between the arch and the river, old shophouses, often weathered, preserve the feel of the town as it once was. Along the riverbank, a promenade runs past restaurants serving freshwater fish. Laos is directly across the river. The whole town is walkable.

practical_info.tip: For a longer trip, tuk-tuks wait near the temple.

activities.text: Small town, wide choice of street food: That Phanom’s night market sets up every evening north of the temple. Stalls line the road running alongside the large ponds. Among the offerings are fried frogs. It’s the easiest option for dinner in That Phanom.

practical_info.tip: Come at dusk and bring small bills and coins.

map_keywords: Wat Roi Phra Phutthabat Phu Manorom

visits.text: Showing its age a little, Ho Kaeo Mukdahan Tower remains the city’s best observation point. Standing 65.5 m tall, it was built in 1996 to mark 50 years of King Rama IX’s reign. The second floor introduces the province’s eight ethnic groups. On the sixth floor, a terrace offers a full panoramic view of the Mekong and Laos. The tower is open from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.; admission is 50 baht.

An 84 m white Buddha dominates the hill at Wat Roi Phra Phutthabat Phu Manorom, above Mukdahan. You can enter the statue, which has four levels leading up to the roof. A few minutes’ walk away, a green-and-blue naga, 122 m long, faces the Mekong. The viewpoint overlooks the city, the river, and Savannakhet in Laos. The site is open from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., with free admission. A pickup truck from the village takes visitors to the summit in exchange for a donation.

You can see the Second Thai–Lao Friendship Bridge from the riverbank in Mukdahan, near the shrine to the revered naga where residents come to pray. The bridge links Mukdahan with Savannakhet in Laos. It opened in December 2006, financed largely through a Japanese loan. Come in the late afternoon, when the heat eases along the riverbank.

activities.text: If you’re looking for an inexpensive sarong or lightweight pants, head to Mukdahan’s Indochina Market on the Mekong. It is one of the markets established to develop trade between Thailand and Laos. Pots and souvenirs are also sold here. Behind the stalls, a path follows the river, facing Savannakhet. The market is open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., but stay on the path for sunset.

practical_info.tip: Save the market for the end of the day, after the tower and Phu Manorom hill.

visits.text: Head out early for Phu Pha Thoep National Park, 17 km south of Mukdahan: it opens around 7:30 a.m., and the bare rock heats up quickly. The trail through the Hin Thoep rock group crosses a field of mushroom-shaped sandstone formations. Their silhouettes resemble swans, crowns, camels, or crocodiles. Higher up, a viewpoint overlooks Mukdahan, the Mekong, and Laos. Trail markings among the rocks are confusing: follow the signs and bring water.

Fa Mue Daeng Cave, the Cave of Red Hands, preserves around ten handprints painted in red ocher. They were made using a stencil technique: people placed a hand against the rock and sprayed pigment around it. Archaeologists date them to 3,000–5,000 years ago. Reaching the cave requires a hike through the park: ask the staff about the trail before setting out, rather than planning it as a short detour from the Hin Thoep rocks. Look without touching the rock wall.

Three thousand holes: that is the meaning of Sam Phan Bok, a name combining the Thai word for three thousand and the Lao word for holes. This reddish sandstone plateau in the Mekong’s riverbed is riddled with round hollows. The river’s swirling currents carved them over the centuries. It emerges only during the dry season, roughly from December to May. For the rest of the year, it is almost entirely underwater. Come at sunrise or sunset, wearing shoes with good traction.

activities.text: The best overall view of Sam Phan Bok is from the river. Long-tail boats—narrow boats whose engines drive propellers at the end of long shafts—depart from Hat Salueng Beach. The trip lasts about 1 hour and covers 4 km along the rocks. Trips are still possible when part of the plateau is underwater. Expect to pay around 1,000 baht per boat, which can be split among several people.

practical_info.tip: On the plateau, a shared pickup truck serves around ten viewpoints for about 200 baht: the most beautiful rocks are far from the parking lot.

visits.text: If you get up early just once, make it for Pha Taem cliff. It overlooks the Mekong and Laos and faces east, with the sun rising directly ahead. The national park opens as early as 5 a.m. Around New Year’s, crowds gather along the cliff edge. Arrive before dawn with a flashlight.

You’ll then follow a walkway along the base of Pha Taem cliff to see its prehistoric paintings. They are 3,000–4,000 years old. The longest of the four groups stretches for about 180 m and contains more than 300 images in red ocher. They depict hands, animals, fish traps, and an enormous Mekong catfish, considered sacred in local beliefs. The cliff trail is about 4 km long. Allow 2 to 3 hours, and bring water and a hat.

At Sao Chaliang, sandstone pillars support stone caps wider than their bases, like giant mushrooms. The caps consist of harder rock than the bases. Wind and rain therefore wear away the bases faster, leaving the caps balanced on top. A 10-minute loop trail passes beneath the pillars. Admission is covered by the Pha Taem park ticket, which costs 200 baht per foreign adult.

activities.text: For a cool end to the morning, nothing beats Thung Na Mueang Waterfall in Pha Taem park, near the Mekong. Its flow depends on rainfall: favor the rainy season and the beginning of the cool season; it may run dry during the dry season. The site is open from 7 a.m. to 4 p.m., with no additional ticket required. It makes a pleasant break after the paintings, before heading back down to spend the night in Khong Chiam.

practical_info.tip: Keep your closed-toe shoes on for the wet rocks at the water’s edge.

visits.text: Khong Chiam residents have a saying for the meeting of the Mekong and the Mun River: “Khong si poon, Mun si khram”—the Mekong is chalky red, the Mun indigo blue. During the rainy season, the Mekong carries large amounts of silt and turns reddish brown. The Mun, held back a little downstream by the Pak Mun Dam, remains clearer, with a blue-green hue. A distinct line then separates the two waters. During the dry season, it is less noticeable. The best viewpoint is the riverbank at Wat Khong Chiam in the late morning.

Rows of seated Buddhas, a reclining Buddha, and a view down over Laos: Wat Tham Khuha Sawan occupies a cliff at a bend in Route 2222, just before Khong Chiam. In this cave temple, the remains of the monk Luang Pu Kam Khaning Chula Mani, a meditation master, rest in a glass coffin. A giant gong greets visitors at the entrance. The site is always open and admission is free, but wear clothing that provides adequate coverage.

In September and October, a waterfall cascades down the cliff just above Wat Tham Hew Sin Chai, a temple built beneath a rocky overhang near Khong Chiam. In April, it is too dry to see the waterfall. During the dry season, come instead for the temple sheltered beneath the rock. The site is open from 8:30 AM to 6 PM, and admission is free.

activities.text: You can reach the confluence by long-tail boat from the riverbank in Khong Chiam. A few boat operators offer the trip, with prices arranged on-site. During the dry season, low water reveals small wooded islands near the confluence. The boat also takes you right up to the line between the two colors. Agree on the price and duration before boarding.

practical_info.tip: Save the late afternoon for Wat Sirindhorn Wararam, 30 minutes to the south, which is best visited after dark.

visits.text: The best time to visit Wat Sirindhorn Wararam Phu Prao, near Chong Mek, is after dark. A large Tree of Life is painted with phosphorescent pigment on the back wall of the ordination hall. This pigment absorbs daylight, then releases it in the dark, without any lamps. The design begins to glow around 7:30 PM. Arrive an hour before sunset to see the temple in daylight, then wait. The temple closes around 8 PM, and admission is free: bring a flashlight for the way back.

Wat Thung Si Muang, a wooden temple dating to the reign of Rama III (1824–1851), keeps its most unusual feature in the middle of a pond. This is the ho trai, the library of sacred texts, built on stilts. The water kept away termites and insects that ate the palm-leaf manuscripts. The temple was originally built to house a copy of the Buddha’s footprint. It is open from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM, and admission is free.

Every July, beeswax sculptures from the Candle Festival are displayed in Thung Si Muang Park in central Ubon. During the rest of the year, you can see a golden column shaped like a royal barge, decorated with garudas, birds from Hindu and Buddhist legends, and nagas. A more modest monument was erected by former Allied prisoners of war to thank the residents who helped them during World War II. The park is just north of the national museum: visit both on foot.

If you are in Ubon between Wednesday and Sunday, set aside 1 hour 30 minutes for the Ubon Ratchathani National Museum. It occupies the former city hall, a yellow building dating to 1918 that became a museum in 1989. Exhibits include pottery from Isan dating back about 3,000 years and rare Buddha statues. The museum is open from 9 AM to 4 PM. Admission cost 100 baht in 2025.

Next, visit Wat Si Ubon Rattanaram, which the city regards as its founding temple. The grand Candle Festival parade sets off from here in July, at the start of the retreat monks observe during the rainy season. That morning, more than fifty floats carry beeswax sculptures through the city. Remove your shoes before entering the halls.

A piece of India in the heart of Isan: Wat Phra That Nong Bua takes its shape from the Mahabodhi Temple in Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment. Its 56 m white-and-gold stupa was built in 1956 to mark 2,500 years of Buddhism. Inside, golden pillars rise to the top around a seated Buddha. The temple is open from 6:30 AM to 8 PM, and admission is free. Save it for the end of the day.

Beneath the trees, silence: Wat Nong Pah Pong is a forest monastery on the outskirts of Ubon. It was founded by Ajahn Chah (1918–1992), a Thai meditation master. A three-story museum tells the story of his life. The monastery also hosts retreats in vipassana, a form of meditation based on self-observation. It is open from 5 AM to 6 PM, and admission is free. Come dressed in clothing that covers your body.

Wat Pah Nanachat was founded in 1975 by Ajahn Chah in the village of Bung Wai, 15 km from Ubon. It is a monastery for foreigners who want to follow the Thai forest monk tradition. Teaching is in English. Visitors are welcome. To stay there, write well in advance, as places are limited. A meal is offered to the monks every morning at 8 AM: plan your visit for afterward.

activities.text: Start the day with a bowl of kuay chap yuan at Ubon Ocha, a well-known spot in Ubon. This Thai-Vietnamese noodle soup comes with pork, chicken, or Vietnamese sausage. The restaurant also serves eggs cooked in a small skillet and Vietnamese-style bread. It is open from 5:30 AM to 3 PM. Arrive early, before heading to the forest monasteries.

practical_info.tip: Have breakfast before 9 AM: morning is the best time to visit the monasteries.

activities.text: Huk Mun Market, on the banks of the Mun River, is worth a visit on your last evening. Makeshift bars and restaurants set up here, some in old train cars. Concerts liven up the evening. The market is open from 4 PM to midnight, but it gets busiest after 6 PM. Sample small portions of several dishes as you move from stall to stall.

practical_info.tip: Ubon Ratchathani Airport, less than 5 km from the center, has flights to Bangkok’s Don Mueang Airport (Nok Air, Thai AirAsia, Thai Lion Air) and Suvarnabhumi Airport (Thai Airways, Thai VietJet). Return your rental car the evening before if you have an early flight.

seo.h1_title: Mekong Isan in 8 Days: That Phanom, Pha Taem, and Ubon
seo.intro_paragraph: This 8-day road trip follows the Mekong from Nakhon Phanom to Khong Chiam, then ends in Ubon Ratchathani. It takes in Ho Chi Minh’s house, the stupa of That Phanom, Mukdahan’s tower, and the rock formations of Phu Pha Thoep and Sam Phan Bok. Next come Pha Taem’s prehistoric paintings, the temple that glows at night in Phu Prao, and Ubon’s temples.

itineraries.title: Eastern Lanna in 7 Days: Nan, Bo Kluea, Phrae, Phayao
itineraries.subtitle: In 7 days, complete a loop from Nan through the salt wells of Bo Kluea, the teak houses of Phrae, and Phayao Lake.
itineraries.notes: Arrive and depart through Nan Airport, which has connections to Bangkok Don Mueang, as Phrae Airport has had no scheduled flights since 2023. From February to April, smoke from agricultural burning often veils northern Thailand’s skies: check the air quality before you leave.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: November to January, with cool mornings (15 to 19 °C in Nan, around 7 °C at Phu Langka) and afternoons around 30 to 32 °C. Avoid March and April, the hottest months (an average of 37 °C in April) and the smokiest due to agricultural burning, which starts as early as February. From May to October, the rainy season peaks in August, and Doi Phu Kha National Park closes from June to September.

map_keywords: Wat Phra That Chang Kham Nan

visits.text: If you visit just one temple in Nan, choose Wat Phumin. Built in 1596, it has a cross-shaped layout. The building appears to rest on the backs of two nagas, legendary serpent guardians of water. Inside, four Buddha statues sit back-to-back, each facing a doorway. The murals were painted by local artist Nan Bua Phan during the restoration from 1867 to 1875. The most famous, Pu Man Ya Man, shows a man whispering into a woman’s ear. Admission is free from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.: come early to enjoy it in peace.

This palace, built in 1903 for Nan’s second-to-last prince, became the Nan National Museum in 1973. Its most remarkable object is a very dark brown elephant tusk measuring 97 cm long. It rests on a wooden stand shaped like Garuda, the giant bird of Hindu and Buddhist legends. The tusk is said to have been intended for a king of Nan about three centuries ago. Open Wednesday through Sunday, from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., with admission costing 100 baht: don’t save it for a Monday.

Twenty-four sculpted elephants emerge halfway from the base of Wat Phra That Chang Kham, as if carrying the golden chedi on their backs. This chedi, a Buddhist monument housing a relic, dates to 1406. In the prayer hall, rebuilt in 1458, a large seated Buddha in the Lanna style, the art of the former northern kingdom, presides over the room. The temple faces the national museum: visit both on foot; admission is free.

activities.text: End the day at the night market next to Wat Phumin. It takes place just three evenings a week, Friday through Sunday, from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. This is a chance to see the temple again at dusk, then have dinner at the food stalls. If you arrive during the week, save this evening outing for your final stop in Nan.

practical_info.tip: Market held Friday through Sunday only, from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m.

visits.text: You might think you were in a canyon in the American West, yet Sao Din Na Noi lies 60 km south of Nan. These earth pillars, known to locals as Hom Chom, were formed by erosion from water and wind. The softer layers were swept away, while the harder ones remained standing. Come early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light accentuates their contours.

activities.text: Continue walking to Kok Suea, the “tiger enclosure,” where earthen walls form a natural enclosure. Allow 1 to 2 hours for the entire site, which is open from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. It is part of Si Nan National Park: admission costs 100 baht for foreign visitors and also covers Doi Samer Dao.

practical_info.tip: During the dry season, check access: in April 2026, the province banned entry to nine national forests in Na Noi and Wiang Sa districts to combat fires.

map_keywords: Wat Phra That Cho Hae Phrae

visits.text: Khum Chao Luang, the residence of Phrae’s last reigning prince, has 72 doors and windows framed in carved wood. Built in 1892, this two-story brick building blends European style with that of Lanna, the former northern kingdom. The palace was also used to administer justice. At its center, a room with no light held prisoners considered the most dangerous. Admission is free from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.; allow at least 1 hour.

The pale pink Vongburi House features finely cut teak decorations on its gables, balconies, and windows. It was built in 1907 for a princely family from Phrae by carpenters from Guangdong, China, assisted by local craftspeople. Inside, antique furniture, silverware, and family papers tell the story of the teak trade era. Those papers include bills of sale for enslaved people. Admission costs 30 baht; posted hours are 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday through Saturday.

Make your way around Phrae’s city walls, which stand about 7 m high and encircle the old town for nearly 4 km. A moat about twenty meters wide runs along their base. The walls are said to date back more than eleven centuries. Follow them by bike or on foot late in the day, when the heat eases.

In our view, Wat Chom Sawan is Phrae’s most evocative temple, built in the Burmese style. Its buildings are made almost entirely of teak, the wood that made the city’s fortune. It stands about 1 km from the provincial government headquarters. Visit in the morning, before the heat sets in, then head to Khum Chao Luang.

It looks centuries old, yet Ban Prathapjai House was only built between 1972 and 1976. Its owner brought together 130 teak pillars, made from trunks said to be about three centuries old. Rounding the number down, it is known as the “house of a hundred pillars.” Visit after Vongburi House: the two showcase Phrae’s teak in two very different eras.

A piece of satin fabric gave Wat Phra That Cho Hae its name. According to tradition, it once wrapped the relic kept in the chedi, a hair of the Buddha. This 33 m octagonal chedi, covered in gilded copper plates, crowns a hill about ten kilometers southeast of Phrae. Around 120 steps lined with nagas lead from the parking lot up to the temple grounds. Admission is free: come late in the afternoon, when the copper catches the light.

activities.text: Follow Route 101 toward Nan for 4 km to reach Thung Hong, the village of mo hom. This cotton, dyed a deep indigo blue using a local plant called hom, has become one of Phrae’s symbols. Shops selling shirts, scarves, and bags line both sides of the road. Not every item is hand-dyed: ask before buying.

practical_info.tip: Shops open daily, from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

visits.text: “Phae” means a sparse forest, and “mueang phi” evokes a silent, almost haunted place: Phae Mueang Phi lives up to its name. Across roughly 80 hectares, rain and wind have sculpted earthen pillars, cliffs, and mushroom-shaped rocks. You can explore the park without a real hike, from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.: arrive in the morning, before the heat sets in.

It took 33 years to build the great Buddha at Wat Si Khom Kham, begun in 1491 and completed in 1524. Known as Phra Chao Ton Luang, this seated Buddha of brick and gilded stucco measures about 14 m from knee to knee. Its height varies by source, from 16 to 18.5 m. It is the province’s most revered Buddha image. The temple stands beside Kwan Phayao Lake and is open from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.: visit before your lakeside walk.

Ho Watanatham Nithat, Phayao’s cultural exhibition hall, helps you understand the city before a lakeside walk. Displays include historical objects, documents, old photographs, and accounts of local history. Phayao was once a city-state, founded nine to ten centuries ago. The hall is about 1 km from Wat Si Khom Kham: allow 45 minutes.

At sunset, the waters of Kwan Phayao turn orange beside the city. This lake covers about 20 km² but is only about 1.5 m deep. It occupies a natural basin. Its water level rose after 1941, when a sluice gate, a kind of small dam, was completed on the Ing River. Around 50 species of fish live here. Rent a bike to follow the bike paths along the shore, lined with restaurants.

If the sky is clear, head up to Wat Analayo Thipphayaram, a temple perched on the slopes of Doi Busarakham, the hill overlooking Phayao. Plan a round trip by car from Phayao for this visit. Its terraces offer views of the city and Kwan Phayao Lake. Morning is best, when the air is cooler and the light is clearer for photos.

activities.text: Take a boat to Wat Tilok Aram, an ancient temple in the middle of Kwan Phayao. This temple was submerged when the lake’s sluice gate raised the water level in the early 1940s. Today, it is accessible only by boat. Go in the morning or late afternoon: the midday sun is intense on the water.

practical_info.tip: The temple is about 2 km from Wat Si Khom Kham.

activities.text: For us, the highlight of Phayao is an evening stroll along its pedestrian street, known as the walking street. You can eat local food and buy souvenirs made by communities in the province. It is an easy way to have dinner after a day by the lake.

practical_info.tip: Opening nights vary: check when you arrive.

visits.text: Route 1148 has 134 curves over 118 km, and Phu Langka is its highlight. Stop at the roadside Pha Chang Noi viewpoint to see the limestone valley below. The massif rises to about 1,720 m. The sea of clouds, a blanket of mist filling the valleys, is most often visible at sunrise. At midday, a brief stop is enough.

activities.text: Park at Phu Langka Forest Park, where a regular car can reach the nature discovery area. Trails lead from there for observing the forest and its birds. Doi Phu Lom, a nearby peak at about 1,600 m, offers a 360-degree view. Some very steep upper tracks require a 4x4.

practical_info.tip: Park open from 5 a.m. to 6 p.m.

visits.text: Three overlapping wood-shingle roofs crown Wat Ton Laeng, descending almost to its walls. This roughly 200-year-old temple is built in the Tai Lue style, named after a Tai-speaking people with a strong presence in the Pua Valley. It stands on a peninsula between the Pua and Khwang Rivers. The hall is sometimes closed for lack of visitors: the roof alone makes the detour worthwhile.

The best view of the Pua Valley is from Wat Phuket, a modern temple about 3 km east of town. It also houses a school for young monks. Head up in the late afternoon, when the low-angle light brings out the rice fields and farms on the valley floor.

activities.text: Walk among the rice fields of Ban Sila Laeng and Silaphet, two villages in the Pua Valley 7 km apart. From September to November, the fields turn from vivid green to harvest gold. Stay on the paddy dikes, the low earthen banks separating the fields, and ask before entering a cultivated plot.

practical_info.tip: Best time for the rice fields: September through February.

activities.text: Ban Hia, near Pua, keeps traditional Tai Lue weaving alive at the Phaeo Phafai workshop. This is the place to see how the fabrics sold in the valley are made. In central Pua, other shops sell textiles from the Lue and the Hmong, a mountain people: compare before buying.

practical_info.tip: Compare prices at the workshop and the shops in the town center before buying.

activities.text: If the heat builds, head to Sila Phet Waterfall in Ban Pa Tong, in Pua District. The water cascades down several tiers, and you can swim here. Bring sandals that stay securely on your feet on wet rocks.

practical_info.tip: Swimming is possible; avoid it after heavy rain.

to_next_leg.road_type: Route 1256, a narrow, winding mountain road

visits.text: The Nan and Pua rivers rise in Doi Phu Kha National Park, which has protected around 1,700 km² since 1999. The park takes its name from Doi Phu Kha, a 1,980 m peak. On the road from Pua to Bo Kluea, about 5 km from the park headquarters, a viewpoint overlooks the ridges. Admission: 200 baht per foreign adult.

activities.text: Clusters of pink flowers identify the chomphu phu kha, a rare tree that grows nowhere else in Thailand outside this park. It blooms from January to early March, especially in February. The nature trail named after it forms a 2 km loop that takes about 1 hour 30 minutes to walk. The longer 4 km loop takes 3 hours.

practical_info.tip: The park closes every year from June 1 to September 30.

to_next_leg.road_type: Narrow Route 1256, with steep drop-offs and sharp turns

visits.text: Far from any coast, deep in the mountains, Bo Kluea nevertheless makes its living from salt. Since the days of the Kingdom of Nan, families have drawn brine—water with a very high salt content—from wells. Bamboo pipes carry it to vats, then it is boiled over a wood fire until white crystals form. Salt is not produced during the rainy season or Buddhist Lent, the monks’ annual retreat: visit between October and February.

activities.text: Continue about ten kilometers north of Bo Kluea to the village of Sapan and its namesake waterfall. Near the waterfall, you can stay in a hut or camp in a tent. Make this detour the evening before or early in the morning, before setting off for Nan.

practical_info.tip: Route 1081 toward Nan is winding and dotted with viewpoints and cafés: leave before noon.

to_next_leg.road_type: Mountain Route 1081, with viewpoints and cafés

visits.text: People born in the Year of the Rabbit consider Wat Phra That Chae Haeng the temple of their zodiac sign. Founded in the 14th century east of the Nan River, it houses a gilded chedi about 55 m tall containing a relic of the Buddha. Two nagas with heads reaching about 4 m high flank the walkway. Free admission from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., 3 km from the center via Route 1168.

End the day at Wat Phra That Khao Noi, on a hill southwest of the city. A 9 m gilded Buddha in a standing, walking pose was erected here in 1999. The temple itself dates to 1487. Its viewpoint overlooks the city and mountains: this is the place in Nan to watch the sunset. Free admission, from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m.

seo.h1_title: Eastern Lanna in 7 Days: Nan, Bo Kluea, Phrae, Phayao
seo.intro_paragraph: This 7-day loop starts and ends at Nan Airport, taking you through the provinces of Nan, Phrae, and Phayao in the eastern part of the former Kingdom of Lanna. You will see the murals of Wat Phumin, the earth pillars of Sao Din, the teak houses of Phrae, and Kwan Phayao Lake. Mountain routes 1148, 1256, and 1081 then lead to the salt wells of Bo Kluea.
seo.seo_hook: Wat Phumin’s murals, Phrae’s teak houses, Kwan Phayao Lake, and Bo Kluea’s salt wells: a 7-day loop through eastern Lanna, starting in Nan.
